ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Cecita Lake source straddles the northern and central side of the Sila Massif in central Calabria (Sila Greca and Sila Grande). The Sila Massif is a mountainous plateau that reaches 1500 m above sea level and that overlies the Ionian subduction (Faccenna et al., 2005). This source is a WSW-dipping normal fault located east of the main extensional axis that runs along the southern Apennines.
Historical catalogues (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2016) show a remarkable concentration of damaging earthquakes around this area. As a matter of fact, these Calabrian earthquakes are among the strongest in Italy's long seismic history (Guidoboni et al., 2007; Rovida et al., 2016). In particular, the southwestern region of the Sila Massif has been struck by the 27 March 1638 event (Mw 7.1; Calabria centrale), the eastern region by the 25 April 1836 (Mw 6.2; Calabria settentrionale), and the southern region by the 8 June 1638 (Mw 6.8; Crotonese). Concerning the 8 June 1638 earthquake, and based on the study of Galli and Bosi (2003), we maintain that its epicenter lies within the Sila Piccola Massif, shifted westward respect to the macroseismically derived one. Our degree of knowledge on macroseismic effects of the 8 June 1638 event is limited because of the Sila mountainous and uninhabited region. This may have resulted in an intensity pattern of the June 1638 earthquake only partially complete, and hence in the mislocation of its epicenter.
Instrumental catalogues (e.g. ISIDe Working Group, 2016) show a scattered distribution of intermediate seismicity (Mw ca. 4) having depths ranging between 10 and 20 km in the Sila Massif, e.g. 23 July 1955 (Mw 4.6), 30 March 1991 (Mw 4.0), 27 April 1996 (Mw 4.8), 26 April 2007 (Mw 4.0), and 28 December 2014 (Mw 4.3) events.
The Cecita Lake source is a NNW-striking normal fault dipping toward the westsouthwest. It is interpreted as a result of a south-eastward roll-back of the hinge of the subducting Ionian lithosphere causing extensional collapse of the orogenic belt (see Tiberti et al., 2017 for a summary). The Cecita Lake fault can be considered the northern continuation of Ampollino Lake Fault, an active source located in the Sila Piccola (Galli and Bosi, 2003). The Cecita Lake source has been known for a long time in the literature (Sorriso-Valvo and Tansi, 1996), and defined active during the Pleistocene (Moretti, 2000).
The Cecita Lake Fault is considered active based on morphotectonic analyses (Sorriso-Valvo and Tansi, 1996). The area is currently characterized by the presence of barrier Cecita Lake (created in the 1950's by an arch dam) that occupies the paleo-Cecita lacustrine basin (late lower Pleistocene). This basin, originally draining toward the Ionian Sea, was captured by the Mucone River, a tributary of the Crati River, problably in the Middle Pleistocene (Galli and Bosi, 2003). The present lake lies in the hangingwall of a prominent NNW-SSE fault scarp facing west (Galli and Bosi, 2003). The expected cumulative vertical deformation field caused by sustained slip on this fault mimics the shape of a trough and fits the averall pattern of long-term deformation revealed by geological and geomorphic observations.
The Cecita Lake fault is not associated with any historical earthquake of the seismic catalogue.
This extensional fault is bounded to the north and south by two main transverse strike-slip structures, known as Cetraro-Rossano Line (Auct.; Del Ben, 1993; Moretti and Guerra, 1997) and Vette Line (Auct.; e.g. Moretti, 2000), respectively.
The strike was based on geological observations. The dip was inferred from geological considerations. The rake was assumed to represent pure extensional fault, based on geodynamic considerations. The minimum and maximum depth was based on surface geology and was inferred from geological and seismological considerations, respectively. The slip rate was inferred from regional geodynamic data. Maximum magnitude was based on the strongest earthquake occurred in the region.
